content: Findings from independent product assessments, including evaluations conducted under the WHO International Scheme to Evaluate Household Water Treatment Technologies, provide critical insights into the performance of water treatment products. In such cases, countries are encouraged to expedite the certification process for household water treatment (HWT) products that meet WHO’s performance standards. Additionally, countries should develop the capacity to conduct complementary validation testing, particularly for locally manufactured HWT products for which assessment data may not yet be available. Regulations should include requirements for the training, skills, and certification of operators responsible for small water supplies. Competent and well-trained operators are essential for ensuring the performance and professionalization of these water supplies. Training programs should address both initial training and demonstrated competence, as well as ongoing capacity development. While it may not be feasible to require the same level of education and qualifications for operators of small water supplies as for those managing larger systems, minimum training and skill levels should be established. Ambitious targets for progressive improvement should also be set to enhance operator competency over time. Regulations should mandate that materials and products used in water supplies comply with established safety standards governing their composition. These standards must be both protective of public health and achievable. In cases where national product testing and certification systems are not yet in place, regulations should require the use of materials and products approved through other national or international certification schemes. Drinking water comes into contact with various material surfaces during abstraction, treatment, distribution, and storage, which may leach hazardous chemicals, promote microbial growth, or impart undesirable tastes and odors. Examples of such materials include components of boreholes, hand pumps, treatment technologies, pipes, fittings, communal taps, storage tanks, and collection containers. Tanker trucks and water carts may also be relevant in certain contexts. Establishing material safety requirements minimizes the risk of contamination from these materials. The cost implications of applying material safety standards must be carefully considered to balance public health protection with feasibility and affordability. Full compliance with standards may not be immediately achievable for many water supplies, particularly those with existing non-compliant components. Interim operational measures, such as corrosion control for metals like lead and iron, should be promoted while non-compliant components are gradually replaced. Regulatory requirements for material safety should be supported by awareness-raising programs for water suppliers, designers, and builders, emphasizing the importance of using safe materials and providing information on approved products and labeling requirements. Training for surveillance staff may also be necessary to enforce material safety standards effectively. Water safety planning (WSP) is a comprehensive, proactive, and ongoing risk management approach that addresses all steps in the water supply chain, from catchment to consumer. Recommended by WHO since 2004 as the most effective method to ensure the safety of drinking water, WSPs have been widely implemented globally. The process involves engaging the community, assembling a WSP team, describing the water supply system, identifying and assessing hazards and risks, developing and implementing an incremental improvement plan, monitoring control measures, planning for emergencies, and continuously reviewing and improving the WSP. Sanitary inspections (SIs) are on-site evaluations that use checklists to identify priority risk factors that may lead to water contamination. These inspections assess the physical structure of water supply components, operational and maintenance practices, and environmental factors. Identified risks should be managed through remedial actions and ongoing management activities. SIs are a well-established practice and can support more comprehensive WSPs by aiding in hazard identification and monitoring. SI packages, which include checklists, technical fact sheets, and management advice sheets, have been developed for common small water supply technologies and are available in various formats to support their implementation. Small water supplies benefit significantly from proactive risk management, as water quality monitoring is often infrequent, and testing all priority parameters may not be feasible. Contamination is often detected only after consumers have been exposed, and the root cause of contamination may not always be clear. Managing risks to source water quality is particularly important for small supplies with limited or no treatment. Proactive measures, such as source protection and hygiene practices, integration of WASH initiatives, and consideration of climate and equity risks, contribute to improved water safety, climate resilience, and social inclusion.
